dau_driver._lazy Import a package’s exports on first use. Every model in this stack is a ccflow model, and importing ccflow imports csp, pandas and the rest of its stack: about 0.9 s. A package whose __init__ imports its model modules therefore pays all of it just to be imported – including when hydra’s searchpath plugin imports the config package to discover what is installed, which is the slow step in composing a registry and wants none of those names. So a package declares which submodule provides each exported name and this builds the __getattr__ that imports the one submodule the name needs. The names stay importable exactly as before, and a type checker reads them from the TYPE_CHECKING block the package keeps beside the declaration. dau_driver.capability_decode.decode_platform_id(value: int) -> str[source] The platform id as ASCII, or "" when the word is not one. A board that advertises no platform is unknown, not dpv1: substituting a default here once reported a dead aperture (all-ones on every word) as a working Artix, and the platform id selects the part, the pricing and the constraints downstream.

dau_driver.capability_decode.decode_register_map_version(value: int) -> dau_core.registers.RegisterMapVersion[source] Decode the register-map version word. An all-ones read means NOT ADVERTISED — the same normalization the capability words use — not a version. Two readers used to disagree on exactly this word: one mapped it to (0, 1), a plausible-looking old shell, while the other ran it through from_u32 and got (65535, 65535), which compares GREATER than the capability-word version and so read words the shell never decoded. A sentinel below every real version makes both readers agree and keeps those offsets unread.

BOTH halves are always written, including a zero high half. A design whose master is wider than 32 bits keeps the high half across a LOW write, so writing only LOW inherits whatever the previous job left and quietly addresses the wrong region. dau_driver.fleet.run_scan_batches_fleet(devices, batches: collections.abc.Iterable[dau_driver.scan_execution.ScanBatch], *, per_key_state: bool, input_regions: tuple[int, int], row_bytes: int, collect: collections.abc.Callable[[Any], Any], timeout_seconds: float = 60.0, progress=None, weights: collections.abc.Sequence[float] | None = None, poll_yield_seconds: float | None = None) -> list[FleetScanResult][source] Run one independent scan pipeline per device over a shared lazy input. Each batch is pulled exactly once by whichever device pipeline demands it. With weights=None this is pure demand-driven scheduling and naturally self-balances by device throughput. Weights use weighted round-robin only to pre-bias each shared pull toward the requested relative device shares; batches remain lazy and are never partitioned or queued ahead. Results are returned in global batch order as frozen FleetScanResult records. Each record retains the exact device object so the caller can recover which card produced its collect value. input_regions is reused as device-local addresses, never shared memory. per_key_state is required and must be False. dau_driver.handle_table The host end of the shell’s handle table: the binding between the StorageAllocator’s bookkeeping and the device aperture that enforces it. dau_driver.storage hands out generation-checked handles, and dau_driver.scan_execution.run_resident_scan() runs jobs over rows already on the device – but by RAW ADDRESS, which is the exposure the table exists to close. A raw address survives its allocation: free the region, hand the space to someone else, and the old address still reads perfectly. It just reads the new tenant’s bytes, and no layer above can tell that from an answer. A handle cannot do that. The allocator’s generation is programmed into the slot, a job names (id, generation) instead of an address, and a resolution that disagrees REFUSES the job – the reader never issues a beat. That refusal arrives here as HandleFaultError, never as results, so a caller cannot mistake it for a job that ran and summed nothing. TWO AUTHORITIES, deliberately different: install trusts the HOST. class dau_driver.handle_table.HandleTable(device, allocator: dau_driver.storage.StorageAllocator, *, capacity: int)[source] One allocator’s slots, mirrored into one device’s handle table. capacity is the built shell’s handle_table_capacity. It is not read off the device: a table is hardware, planned into the design and priced with it, and there is no register that advertises it – an id past the end is a fault (BAD_ID), not a discovery. Passing the design’s number here turns that fault into a refusal on the host, where the mistake still costs nothing.

install(handle: dau_driver.storage.StorageHandle) -> None[source] Program handle’s grant into slot handle.id. The allocator resolves the handle first and that resolution is the authority: base, length and generation are taken from the LIVE record, so a handle the host no longer believes in never becomes a grant the device does. Raises StaleHandleError if it will not resolve – that is a host bug, and papering over it would install exactly the stale grant the table exists to refuse.

free(handle: dau_driver.storage.StorageHandle) -> None[source] Drop slot handle.id out of liveness, so nothing resolves through it until it is installed again. Deliberately unconditional on the allocator: freeing a slot can only make the table refuse MORE, so it is safe whether or not the host has released the span yet. A version that demanded a live handle would refuse the call from a caller who freed host-side first, and leave the device answering for a region that has already been handed on.

arm(handle: dau_driver.storage.StorageHandle) -> None[source] Name the handle the NEXT job resolves, in place of an input address. Checked against nothing on purpose. A stale handle has to reach the table or the table is never what refused it – and a host that pre-validates here proves only that the host agrees with itself.

run_resident_scan(handle: dau_driver.storage.StorageHandle, *, row_count: int, row_bytes: int, collect, repeats: int = 1, timeout_seconds: float = 60.0, poll_yield_seconds: float | None = None) -> list[source] run_resident_scan() with the raw address replaced by a handle: arm once, then run the job repeats times over rows already on the device, uploading nothing. poll_yield_seconds sleeps that long between JOB_STATUS polls instead of spinning. Measured on dpv1 (2026-09-27) it is the wrong default for a Python caller: any sleep, 0 included, hands the GIL to another thread and the poll waits out a full switch interval per iteration, milliseconds on a job that runs for less; the contention it was meant to relieve was elsewhere. It stays for a caller whose other threads do not hold the GIL. Returns one collect(device) per repeat. Raises HandleFaultError the moment the shell refuses – results for the repeats that did run are dropped with it, because a run whose dataset stopped being the caller’s part way through is not a partial answer.

dau_driver.pipeline_execution.device_job_capacity(device) -> tuple[int, int][source] (input rows, output records) ONE job may stage on the RESIDENT shell. These are the shell’s BRAM depths, and the host used to carry them as module constants – one pair for the grouped shell and one for the bar shell, both compiled in. Every shell was therefore batched against the depths of whichever shell the constants were written for, and a shell built with a different depth would have been sliced to the wrong size with nothing to say so. The shell advertises them from register map 0.3. Refuses when the shell advertises nothing, exactly like the lane count: a 0.2 or earlier shell does not decode these offsets, and a host that guessed here would be reintroducing the constants this replaced. Reads the two capacity words directly rather than taking a whole identity snapshot: this sits on the per-job path, and a snapshot is ~25 MMIO reads where three will do. Not cached, because a device can be reflashed inside one session – the flywheel does exactly that – and a cached capacity would then describe the previous shell.

dau_driver.storage Host-side storage allocation over a platform’s declared tiers. The dumb half of the allocation lifecycle in STORAGE_AND_NOC.md: the host owns an allocator per shared tier and hands out generation-checked handles; tiles consume grants and never allocate. The handle table this allocator maintains is exactly what a future allocator tile would drive — the API does not change when it does. Freed storage is never readdressed: free bumps the handle’s generation, and a stale handle raises instead of resolving to reused memory. Exhaustion raises before anything is staged. stage/resolve take any object with write_dma (the duck-typed device convention). dau_driver.verify_advertisement Check that a device is running the design a build manifest describes. A programming ladder that only checks the endpoint reappeared cannot tell a successful reprogram from a failed one. The FPGA falls back to its flash-resident design when a volatile program does not take, so the endpoint comes back either way, with the same vendor and device id, at the same address. On 2026-08-06 a dpv1 SRAM program failed silently for exactly this reason: the programmer exited zero without writing, the plan saw an endpoint, disarmed its deadman, and reported success while the board kept running the previous design. Reads the manifest as text and pulls the embedded JSON rather than importing the build package: this runs on a bench host where only the driver may be installed.

dau_driver.verify_advertisement.build_id_mismatch(snapshot, spec_hash: str | None, *, required: bool = False) -> str | None[source] The EXACT check, when both sides carry it: does the shell’s BUILD_ID match the spec hash of the design the manifest describes? This is what the advertised capability words cannot do. They are a coarse projection — most designs share a word tuple with several others, and q19-scan and q19-packed-wide are identical across all four — so a word-level match is consistent with the board running a different design. A BUILD_ID match is not. Returns None when the check does not apply: no spec hash in the manifest, or a shell that advertises BUILD_ID 0 (unstamped, which every shell built before stamping existed does). Absence is reported by the caller rather than treated as agreement — an unstamped shell is a weaker verification, not a passing one.

dau_driver.verify_advertisement.advertisement_mismatches(snapshot, contract: collections.abc.Mapping[str, Any]) -> tuple[str, ...][source] Every advertised word where the device and the contract disagree. A word the contract does not record is SKIPPED rather than treated as zero: an older manifest that predates a word should not fail a device that advertises it. A word the contract records and the device does not match is a mismatch, which is the case that matters. Raises when the contract records no NON-ZERO word. All-zero is what a dead or undecoded register aperture reads back as — the driver normalizes all-ones to zero precisely so a dead word advertises nothing — so a contract of all zeros would match a board that is not answering at all. Such a contract cannot identify a design, and saying so is the only safe answer; silently passing is the failure this module exists to prevent.

test_handle_table.test_a_freed_handle_is_refused(tmp_path) -> None Freeing the slot stops it resolving even though the memory is untouched and the base the handle used to mean still reads fine.

test_handle_table.test_a_recycled_slot_refuses_the_previous_generation(tmp_path) -> None THE CASE THE TABLE EXISTS FOR. The allocator recycles the id, so the second allocation lands in the same SLOT over a different region. The first caller’s handle is byte-for-byte what it always was and its base still reads – the generation is the only thing that can refuse it. It does, and the reissued handle reaches the new tenant’s region, proving the slot was really reused underneath.

test_handle_table.test_an_unarmed_job_handle_is_refused(tmp_path) -> None Generation zero is one the allocator never issues, so a host that starts a job without arming a handle is refused rather than quietly reading slot zero – which is live here, and would otherwise answer.

test_handle_table.test_a_job_longer_than_the_grant_is_refused(tmp_path) -> None The grant bounds the read: asking past it would walk into whatever follows the region, the same wrong answer by a different route.

test_handle_table.test_repeats_amortize_one_staging_over_many_jobs(tmp_path) -> None The residency claim itself, through a handle: the rows are staged once and the job runs against the same grant repeatedly, arming it once.

test_handle_table.test_an_off_grid_length_is_refused_before_it_becomes_a_length_gate_fault(tmp_path) -> None The shell’s 0xFE length gate fires before the table is asked, so an off-grid length would arrive as a fault that says nothing about the handle.

test_no_board_geometry_constants Board geometry does not live in this package. The rule the docs state repeatedly: hardware access is board/host configuration, never code defaults. A module constant naming an address, a region size, or a device’s capacity is a second source of truth for something the platform already declares, and the two drift the first time a board differs — which is exactly how a host ended up assuming four lanes on a shell that advertises its own count, and how one board’s DDR layout ended up applied to another behind a memory_bytes > 1 << 32 conditional. Wire and record shapes are NOT board geometry and stay: how many bytes a bar record occupies is a property of the format both sides compile against, not of the board it runs on. The two are easy to confuse, so this pins the distinction explicitly rather than leaving it to a reviewer’s judgement. Asserted EXACTLY and in both directions: remove a constant without tightening this list and the test fails; add one without justifying it here and the test fails. The list is expected to shrink. t: Storage handles: why a generation instead of a pointer
s: The bug this design does not have
x: A conventional allocator hands back an address. Free it, allocate again, and the new allocation may sit at the same address, so a stale reference to the old one now reads and writes storage that belongs to something else. On a host that is a use-after-free. On a device it is worse, because there is no page table to fault: the DMA succeeds, the data is wrong, and nothing anywhere reports a problem. The fix is not to hand out addresses. A handle is (id, generation) plus a snapshot of its placement, and resolve(handle) returns an address only if the allocator’s live record still matches. Freeing bumps the generation, so a stale handle raises StaleHandleError instead of resolving: handle 0 generation 1 is stale, forged, or from another allocator (current generation: 1); freed storage is never readdressed That sentence is the invariant: freed storage is never readdressed through an old name. A few other checks follow from it. A double free faults, because free resolves first. A handle from another allocator faults, because the allocator token does not match. And a handle whose fields were tampered with faults, because the comparison is against the live record, not the caller’s copy.

t: Storage handles: why a generation instead of a pointer
s: The live record is always authoritative
x: Every operation reads the allocator’s record rather than the handle’s own base and capacity. stage checks the payload length against the live grant. free returns the live span to the free list. The reason is not malicious callers. A frozen handle passed around a program is a copy of facts that were true when it was issued, and the allocator is the only thing that knows whether they still are. Trusting the copy would make the generation check pointless: you would validate the identity and then act on unvalidated data.

t: Storage handles: why a generation instead of a pointer
x: The allocator could instead never reuse an id: a monotonic counter, no recycling, and no need for a generation. That would be simpler, but it would not match the hardware. The shell’s handle table has a fixed number of slots, because that is what fits in BRAM. Slots get reused, and the generation is what makes reuse safe. Because the software allocator already followed the same rule, the API did not change when the table arrived in hardware: HandleTable programs a slot straight from the allocator’s live record, and nothing above it changed. The general rule: shape the simple software half of a lifecycle like the hardware half that will replace it, not like whatever is easiest in Python.

t: Storage handles: why a generation instead of a pointer
x: The division of labour is that the host owns an allocator per shared storage tier and hands out grants, and tiles consume grants and never allocate. There is no device-side allocation path today and the API is designed so there does not need to be one later. Reserved regions are how the fixed parts of the map stay out of the way. Lane output windows and fixed staging areas are carved out of the free list at construction, so nothing can be allocated on top of them. A reserved region outside the tier, or with a non-positive size, raises immediately, so a wrong memory map fails at construction rather than by handing out an address inside a lane’s output window and corrupting a result three jobs later.

t: Storage handles: why a generation instead of a pointer
s: Why the device has to make the check
x: A host-side check is enough right up until the device reads on its own. A job over rows already resident on the device names the region it should read, and a raw address outlasts its allocation: free the region, hand the space to someone else, and the old address still reads without error. It reads the new owner’s bytes, and no layer above can tell that from a real answer. HandleTable closes that by programming the grant into a slot and letting the job name (id, generation) instead of an address. When the table disagrees with a resolution, the shell does not start the job (the reader never issues a beat), and the host gets a HandleFaultError, never results, so a caller cannot mistake it for a job that ran and summed nothing. It is also why arm validates nothing. The stale handle has to reach the device, or the table never checks it, and the fault would be a host-side assertion presented as a hardware one.

x: The guard is a dau-utils tool, not part of this package: sudo python -m dau_utils.deadman arm --timeout <seconds> sudo python -m dau_utils.deadman status sudo python -m dau_utils.deadman disarm dau-driver neither implements nor depends on it. dau_utils is a separate prerequisite on the bench host, and nothing here will tell you it is missing. s: Disarm only after the device answers
x: The ordering matters more than the arming does. A programmed board is not healthy because programming returned. It is healthy because the device it produced identified itself afterwards. So the ladder is: arm, do the destructive span, discover the device, read the magic word, read back the identity block, compare it against what was built, and only then disarm. Verification steps come before the disarm on purpose, so an uncaught exception in a verify step reboots the host. That is the intended behaviour. The alternative is the incident this ordering exists to prevent, where a plan saw an endpoint, disarmed, and reported success while the board kept running the previous design. s: Guard against addressing past the end of memory
x: An address beyond the device’s memory does not fail. It wraps to the bottom, and you read or overwrite the wrong region without any error. Tell the handle how big its memory is, then program addresses through the method form: import dataclasses from dau_core.registers import RegisterOffset device = dataclasses.replace(device, memory_bytes=platform.memory.size_bytes) device.write_address_register(RegisterOffset.INPUT_ADDRESS_LOW, RegisterOffset.INPUT_ADDRESS_HIGH, address) RegisterAccessError is then raised for an address at or past the limit. Left as None, the caller is trusted: the guard is only as good as the fact, and an invented default would either reject valid addresses or give false confidence. The module-level write_address function reads memory_bytes off the device by default. Pass an integer to override the limit, or None to disable the check entirely, but only on purpose: the default is what makes the guard apply to callers who never thought about it.

s: Program a 64-bit address into a register pair
x: Device addresses are wider than a register, so they are written as a LOW/HIGH pair: from dau_core.registers import RegisterOffset from dau_driver.device import write_address write_address(device, RegisterOffset.INPUT_ADDRESS_LOW, RegisterOffset.INPUT_ADDRESS_HIGH, address) Always write both halves, which is what write_address does even when the high half is zero. Pass the offsets explicitly rather than deriving low + 4. The job pair is adjacent, but a NoC lane’s is not: its high half is at 0x14, because 0x04 is the result length. write_address is a function, not a method, because devices here are duck-typed: test fakes and alternative transports implement write_register without subclassing DauDevice.

x: The shells read a DAU stream batch: a header, one descriptor per column, optional operation descriptors, and 64-byte-aligned payloads. Build one from fixed-width, null-free columns: import struct from dau_core.stream import LogicalType, OperationCode, OperationDescriptor, output_type_for from dau_driver.stream_codec import RecordBatchColumn, StreamEncoder symbols = [1, 1, 2] prices = [1050, 1075, 990] columns = ( RecordBatchColumn(field_id=0, logical_type=LogicalType.INT32, payload=struct.pack(f"<{len(symbols)}i", *symbols)), RecordBatchColumn(field_id=1, logical_type=LogicalType.INT32, payload=struct.pack(f"<{len(prices)}i", *prices)), ) operation = OperationDescriptor( operation_id=0, opcode=OperationCode.SUM, input_column_id=1, output_field_id=0, output_type=output_type_for(OperationCode.SUM), accumulator_width_bits=64, ) encoded = StreamEncoder.encode_record_batch(columns, row_count=len(prices), operations=(operation,)) For a single column, StreamEncoder.encode_column(logical_type, payload, row_count=..., operations=...) is the one-column form. Nulls are rejected: the format has no validity bitmap, so null_count must be zero. Drop or fill upstream.

Pass a generator and the runner pulls each batch just before staging it, so whatever work the iterator does happens concurrently with the running job: def batches(): for chunk in chunks: yield ScanBatch(payload=encode(chunk), row_count=len(chunk)) results = run_scan_batches(device, batches(), per_key_state=False, ...) Strategy Use when Guarantee Position slicing (build ScanBatch yourself) The composition is stateless per batch. None beyond batch size. key_partitioned_scan_batches The composition carries per-key state across a batch. Each key lands in exactly one batch. key_range_scan_batches The composition uses a hash-mode grouped tile with a fixed key capacity. Each batch holds at most key_capacity distinct keys, and each key lands in exactly one batch.

from dau_driver.scan_execution import key_partitioned_scan_batches batches = key_partitioned_scan_batches( records, batch_count=8, key=lambda record: record.symbol, encode=encode_rows, ) Assignment is longest-processing-time-first: the largest key group goes to the currently smallest batch. Records must arrive ordered by key: a key appearing in two runs raises ValueError. Record order within each key is preserved. The first iteration consumes one complete grouping pass, because LPT needs every group size before it can assign. After that, each batch’s payload is built only when that batch is requested. Key groups are indivisible, so one hot key can dominate a batch. Pass per_key_state=True when running these. The runner requires it for a stateful composition and checks that the batches came from this function. A position-sliced iterable raises ValueError rather than splitting a key’s state without telling you.

from dau_driver.scan_execution import key_range_scan_batches batches = key_range_scan_batches( records, key_capacity=512, key=lambda record: record.symbol, encode=encode_rows, ) Size the batches so the hash table cannot overflow rather than reacting to the device’s GROUP_CAPACITY_EXCEEDED close-out. The key space is partitioned into ranges of key_capacity keys and one batch is emitted per range. Records need not arrive in key order here, and arrival order is preserved within each batch. The hash table needs no key ordering, and imposing one would give up the staging freedom the tile exists to provide. The trade is a counting pass over every key before the first batch, and row counts that may be uneven: key ranges are equal in keys, not in rows. Because each key lands in exactly one batch, combining the per-batch group records is a plain concatenation. If your batches came from somewhere else, use dau_core.operators.merge_hash_grouped for the general additive merge instead.

Each repeat programs the address and length, starts the job, waits, and calls collect, so you get one result per repeat rather than one merged answer, so you can check that a rerun returns identical results instead of assuming it. The address must be on the 64-byte DMA grid, and it is raw: it outlives the allocation it came from. Bias the split with weights, one positive, finite value per device, to pre-weight each shared pull toward the requested relative shares. Batches stay lazy and are never queued ahead. per_key_state must be False. A stateful composition cannot run on a fleet at all: batches go to whichever card is free, so a key’s rows split across cards that never see each other’s state. x: Both runners raise PipelineJobError when a job’s status neither reports DONE before timeout_seconds nor reports an error flag: scan job 3 timed out (status=0x0) A device-side error flag is raised the same way, with LAST_ERROR included: scan job 3 failed: status=0x3 last_error=2 Raise timeout_seconds for large batches; the default is 60 seconds. x: Capabilities are decoded from the device’s own register block, so they describe the bitstream that is loaded, not the driver. Run: dma = device.capabilities.dma print("alignment_bytes: ", dma.alignment_bytes) print("max_transfer_bytes:", dma.max_transfer_bytes) for operator in device.capabilities.operators: print(operator.opcode.name, [t.name for t in operator.input_types], "->", operator.output_type.name) Output: alignment_bytes: 64 max_transfer_bytes: 4096 SUM ['INT32'] -> INT64 MIN ['INT32'] -> INT64 MAX ['INT32'] -> INT64 COUNT ['INT32'] -> UINT64 Two things are worth noticing. The DMA constraints are facts you will have to respect in Step 4. And the operator list is typed: SUM over INT32 produces INT64, and asking for any other output type is an error the driver catches before touching the bus.

s: Step 3: Read the identity and status registers
x: Register access goes through the same transport. Preload a few values so the fake has something to report, then read them back. Run: from dau_core.registers import DAU_MAGIC_WORD, RegisterOffset transport.registers[int(RegisterOffset.MAGIC)] = DAU_MAGIC_WORD transport.registers[int(RegisterOffset.STATUS)] = 0b0111 transport.registers[int(RegisterOffset.ROWS_LOW)] = 1_000_000 transport.registers[int(RegisterOffset.BATCHES)] = 12 print("magic:", hex(device.read_register(RegisterOffset.MAGIC))) status = device.read_status() print("status:", bin(status.raw_status), "last error:", status.last_error) print(device.read_counters()) Output: magic: 0x44415531 status: 0b111 last error: 0 DeviceCounters(h2c_bytes=0, c2h_bytes=0, rows=1000000, batches=12, stalls=0) 0x44415531 is the DAU magic word, which is how discovery tells a DAU shell from any other XDMA bitstream. DeviceStatus holds the status word as read, and the counters are 64-bit values read as two 32-bit register accesses.

s: Step 4: Check the register path is healthy
x: A dead AXI-lite path does not fail; it returns all ones, which looks like a perfectly good number. check_bar_health() is the check for that. Run: device.check_bar_health() print("BAR health: ok") Output: BAR health: ok Now break it and watch what happens: from dau_driver import UnhealthyBarError transport.registers[int(RegisterOffset.MAGIC)] = 0xFFFF_FFFF try: device.check_bar_health() except UnhealthyBarError as exc: print("UnhealthyBarError:", exc) transport.registers[int(RegisterOffset.MAGIC)] = DAU_MAGIC_WORD Output: UnhealthyBarError: MAGIC read all ones from /tmp/xdma0_user; BAR/AXI-lite path may be unhealthy Call this before and after any sequence you care about. It is cheap and it turns a wrong number into a named failure.

s: Step 3: Confine each key to one batch
x: Some scan compositions keep per-key state across a batch, a grouped aggregation for instance. Slicing rows by position would then split a key’s state across two jobs. key_partitioned_scan_batches builds batches where each key lands in exactly one. Run: from dau_driver.scan_execution import key_partitioned_scan_batches transport = FakeTransport() transport.registers[int(RegisterOffset.JOB_STATUS)] = int(JobStatusFlag.DONE) device = fake_device(Path("/tmp"), transport) partitioned = key_partitioned_scan_batches( readings, batch_count=2, key=lambda reading: reading[0], encode=encode, ) results = run_scan_batches( device, partitioned, per_key_state=True, input_regions=(0x0000_0000, 0x0800_0000), row_bytes=ROW_BYTES, collect=collect, timeout_seconds=5.0, ) print("results:", results) Output: results: [48, 48] Six rows across three key groups, balanced into two batches of three. The assignment is longest-processing-time-first: the largest key group goes into the currently smallest batch. Records must arrive ordered by key, and record order within each key is preserved.

t: Run a scan over many batches
x: per_key_state is not advisory. Try running the plain list of batches from Step 1 with it set: try: run_scan_batches( device, batches, per_key_state=True, input_regions=(0x0000_0000, 0x0800_0000), row_bytes=ROW_BYTES, collect=collect, ) except ValueError as exc: print("ValueError:", exc) Output: ValueError: scan composition has cross-batch per-key state; batches must be key-partitioned with key_partitioned_scan_batches A stateful composition only accepts batches that came from key_partitioned_scan_batches. The check is on the batch iterable’s identity, not on a flag you could get wrong, so a position-sliced batch cannot reach a stateful job by accident.

t: Run a scan over many batches
s: Step 5: Bound the distinct keys per batch
x: A different constraint applies to the hash-mode grouped tile: its table holds a fixed number of distinct keys, and a batch presenting more is invalidated by the device. Rather than react to that, size the batches so it cannot happen. Run: from dau_driver.scan_execution import key_range_scan_batches for batch in key_range_scan_batches(readings, key_capacity=2, key=lambda reading: reading[0], encode=encode): print(batch.row_count) Output: 4 2 Two batches: the first holds keys AAA and BBB (four rows), the second holds CCC (two). The key ranges are equal in keys, not in rows, which is why the row counts differ. Because each key lands in exactly one batch, combining the per-batch group records is a plain concatenation. And unlike Step 3, records need not arrive in key order: the hash table needs no key ordering, so arrival order is preserved within each batch.

dau-driver Host I/O for DAU devices: discovery, registers, DMA, and job execution over XDMA Build Status codecov License PyPI dau-driver is the host side of a DAU device. It discovers DAU-compatible XDMA endpoints, reads the canonical register block, decodes the device’s capability advertisement, moves data over H2C/C2H DMA, allocates device storage, and runs the register-contract jobs the shells expose. All device semantics (register offsets, stream framing, capability words, record layouts) come from dau-core; this package owns transport and execution only. Linux hosts use the Xilinx XDMA character devices under /dev. macOS hosts use a DriverKit-based XDMA system extension through IOKit user-client calls, for register access and full H2C/C2H DMA. from pathlib import Path from dau_driver import discover_devices from dau_driver.testing import FakeTransport, fake_device devices = discover_devices() # the XDMA devices under /dev, when a board is installed device = devices[0] if devices else fake_device(Path("."), FakeTransport()) device.check_bar_health() # all-ones reads fail here, not later print(device.name, device.backend) # xdma0 linux-xdma print(device.capabilities.dma) # align

The full documentation is at dau-dev.github.io/dau-driver. Tutorial: Talk to a device without any hardware · Run a scan over many batches. Both drive a device end to end against the fake transport, no board required. How-to guides: Find and check a device · Move data to and from it · Run scan jobs across batches and cards · Allocate device storage · Fence a PCIe operation with the deadman · Develop and contribute. Reference: Device and discovery, including transfers, storage and errors · Execution contracts for stream, scan, pipeline and fleet jobs · Stream codec. Explanation: Why the driver owns almost nothing and where the dau-core boundary sits · Why staging overlaps compute, and when the runner stops · Why storage is handed out as generation-checked handles. The examples directory holds end-to-end host flows (record-batch round trip, stream aggregation, the OHLCV pipeline job) that run against real hardware.

Requires Python 3.12 or newer. pip install dau-driver Wheels are published for CPython 3.12 and 3.13 on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64) and macOS (arm64). Elsewhere pip builds the small native extension from source, which needs a C++ toolchain. On a host with a board, load the Linux XDMA module from kernel/linux-xdma/ or the macOS DriverKit extension from kernel/macos-xdma/; each has its own build and load instructions. Without one, the package still imports and runs against its fake transport. Whoever can open the character devices (Linux) or the user client (macOS) can read and write the card’s memory and registers, so the operating system’s device permissions are the access control.
Apache-2.0, except kernel/linux-xdma/, which is Xilinx’s XDMA reference driver under its own Dual BSD/GPL terms. See kernel/README.md.

Kernel driver sources linux-xdma/: the Xilinx XDMA reference driver from Xilinx/dma_ip_drivers, XDMA/linux-kernel/xdma at upstream commit 14c9f045bad9 (2024-04-04, driver version v2020.2.2 in its version.h), with COPYING, LICENSE and include/libxdma_api.h from the same tree. Sixteen of the twenty-one files are byte-identical to that commit; the other five (cdev_ctrl.c, cdev_sgdma.c, libxdma.h, xdma_cdev.c, xdma_mod.c) carry the changes in linux-xdma-dau.patch: kernel-version guards for the 6.3 vm_flags_set, the 6.4 class_create signature and the 6.5 removal of the vector-I/O helpers (read_iter/write_iter return -EOPNOTSUPP there; the DAU transfer path uses the scalar calls), a flexible array member, and trailing whitespace. The provenance was established by matching every file’s blob hash against upstream history: the import lies between that commit and the next upstream change to the directory (2025-03-04). Build it on the hardware host with make and load it with insmod ./xdma.ko. The module is built on the host it runs on, never copied between hosts. macos-xdma/: the macOS DriverKit system extension and its activator, written for this project. Both drivers expose the card’s memory and registers to whoever can open the device: the /dev/xdma* character devices on Linux, the IOKit user client on macOS. Neither driver checks what a transfer does to the card. The operating system’s device permissions (a udev rule on Linux) are the access control, so grant the device nodes to the user who runs the host software and to nobody else.

The upstream LICENSE (BSD) and COPYING (GPL-2.0) files are included alongside the sources, exactly as they ship in Xilinx/dma_ip_drivers. The Apache-2.0 licence at the root of this repository does not apply to that directory. Everything else in this repository, including macos-xdma/, is Apache-2.0.

XDMA macOS DriverKit Extension This directory contains a macOS DriverKit system extension (dext) that adapts the Xilinx XDMA PCIe driver model for macOS: device matching, BAR register access, and H2C/C2H DMA through the XDMA engines, driven from Python over IOKit user-client calls. Overview The XDMA driver provides: PCI Device Matching: Automatically detects Xilinx XDMA PCIe devices (vendor 0x10ee and 0x1d0f) BAR Register Access: Read/write access to PCIe Base Address Registers for device control DMA Transfers: Host-to-Card (H2C) and Card-to-Host (C2H) transfers through the XDMA descriptor engines Device Information: Query vendor, device, and subsystem IDs The DriverKit service is registered as com.dau-dev.xdma — the one name user-space tools match. (XDMADriver survives only as the dext C++ class name.) The dext sets no user-client entitlement and declares allow-any-userclient-access, so any process on the host that can open the service can read and write the card’s registers and run DMA against host memory it supplies. That is deliberate: the client is an unsigned Python process, and it matches what the Linux character devices give under a permissive udev rule. Whoever can run code on the host can drive the card. Do not install the dext on a machine where that is not acceptable. What the dext does enforce is the shape of a request: the BAR index is one of the six, the offset is 32-bit aligned, and the access lies inside the mapped length of that BAR (recorded at start from GetBARInfo), so a register access cannot reach past the device’s own ranges; DMA lengths and buffers are checked the same way.

The driver automatically matches PCI devices based on vendor and device IDs specified in Info.plist. When a supported device is detected: macOS loads the driver Driver’s Start() method is called Driver opens the PCI device and maps BARs Driver discovers XDMA engines Driver calls SetName("com.dau-dev.xdma") and RegisterService(), making it visible to userspace Userspace opens XDMAUserClient through XDMADriver::NewUserClient
Based on the Xilinx XDMA IP:
User-defined registers for FPGA logic Typical usage: Control, status, data registers

H2C Channels: 0x0000, 0x0100, 0x0200, 0x0300 C2H Channels: 0x1000, 0x1100, 0x1200, 0x1300 Interrupt Block: 0x2000 Config Block: 0x3000 Each DMA channel has: Identifier (0x00) Control (0x04) Status (0x40) Completed descriptors (0x48) SGDMA descriptor address (0x80, 0x84)

Create DMA descriptor with: src_addr = host physical address dst_addr = device offset bytes = transfer size control = 0xAD4B0000 (DESC_MAGIC) Write descriptor address to engine’s SGDMA registers Start engine (set XDMA_CTRL_RUN_STOP in control register) Wait for completion (poll status or interrupt)
Same as H2C but with reversed addresses: src_addr = device offset dst_addr = host physical address

Hardware Host Operations Scripts Run these on the Linux hardware host (see dau-docs GUIDELINES “Hardware Rules” for the mandatory ordering): sudo python -m dau_utils.deadman arm --timeout N (disarm | status) — cancellable auto-reboot guard; arm before ANY PCIe/JTAG-touching sequence, disarm only after the health ladder passes. Pairs with the systemd hardware watchdog (RuntimeWatchdogSec=60 → wdat_wdt on the bench host). Runtime-PM holds, endpoint removal, secondary-bus reset and rescan are NOT scripts here: they are steps of the composed dau-build hardware plans (plan=plans/thunderbolt-hold, plans/thunderbolt-release, plans/recovery, plans/sram-program). Use those. They arm the deadman around the destructive span, take the host lock, carry the platform’s host-access facts, and support a dry run — none of which a bare script does. A hand-run bus reset with no deadman is how the host wedges. dau-xdma-poc.py — DMA write/read/compare bandwidth validation runner (H2C and C2H whole-transfer reads).
